[Gathered by ApprovalReady from official websites on 2026-10-11; a summary, not the source's wording] How to get: Register a company (Pty Ltd) with ASIC (Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC); director IDs are issued by Australian Business Registry Services (ABRS)).
A company is a separate legal entity, so you register it with ASIC to get an Australian Company Number (ACN) before it can trade. Every director must have a director ID before being appointed, and the company pays an annual review fee every year it stays registered.
Timeframe: About 15 minutes online once you have everything ready; confirmation usually within 2 business days if documents are complete and the fee is paid.
Cost: A$636 to register a proprietary company (from 1 July 2026), then a A$342 annual review fee each year. Director IDs are free.
Before you start: Make sure a company suits you: sole traders, partnerships and trusts do not register with ASIC as companies. A company has extra legal duties and ongoing costs.
Before you start: Every director must apply for their own director ID before they are appointed. It is free, done through ABRS, and you keep it for life even if you change companies.
Before you start: To apply for a director ID online you need a Digital ID such as myID with at least Standard identity strength, plus your ATO-held residential address and details from two verification documents (for example a notice of assessment). Giving your TFN is optional but speeds things up.
Before you start: Choose a name that shows legal status (for example 'Example Pty Ltd') and check it on ASIC's name availability search, or let ASIC use your ACN as the name.
Before you start: Decide your state or territory of registration, registered office address and principal place of business.
Before you start: Decide your internal rules: the replaceable rules in the Corporations Act 2001, your own constitution, or a mix.
Before you start: Work out the share structure and members. For each member you need name and address and written consent; for each director and secretary you need full name (including former names), home address, date and place of birth, and signed written consent to act, which you must keep.
Before you start: If the company will trade under a name other than its exact company name, it needs a separate business name registration.
Step 1: Each director gets a director ID. Every proposed director applies for their own director ID through ABRS before the company is registered. Online is fastest: sign in with myID (Standard or Strong), answer the identity questions and submit; your ID appears on screen. If you cannot get a myID with at least Standard strength, ABRS has other ways to apply depending on where you live. (time: Immediate online; cost: Free)
Step 2: Choose and check the company name. Check the name on ASIC's name availability search. You can optionally reserve a name for up to 2 months using ASIC Form 410 if you are not ready to register. (cost: Name reservation fee applies (amount not confirmed); form: Form 410 Application for reservation of a name)
Step 3: Prepare company details and consents. Prepare the registered office and principal place of business addresses, your rules (replaceable rules or constitution), share classes and numbers, member details and written consents, and each officeholder's details and signed consent to act.
Step 4: Register through the Business Registration Service. Apply to register the company (proprietary limited, public, or special purpose) in the Business Registration Service and pay the fee. You can add the company's ABN, GST, PAYG withholding and a business name in the same application. Some cases, such as hiding a residential address or an unlimited company, need a paper form or business service provider instead. (time: About 15 minutes; confirmation usually within 2 business days; cost: A$636 (proprietary company, from 1 July 2026); form: Business Registration Service)
Step 5: Receive your ACN, certificate and corporate key. The Business Registration Service emails the ACN and certificate of registration. ASIC posts the corporate key to the registered office; you need it to use ASIC's company officeholder portal. Show the company name wherever the company trades publicly, and put the name and ACN on required documents.
Step 6: Do the annual review every year. ASIC sends an annual statement after your review date (usually the registration anniversary). Check and update the company details, pass a solvency resolution, and pay the annual review fee. Keep company records and the share register up to date throughout the year. (time: Each year; late fees apply if not paid within 2 months of the review date; cost: A$342 (proprietary company, from 1 July 2026))
Fee: Register a proprietary company: A$636.00 (From 1 July 2026 (up from A$611))
Fee: Annual review fee, proprietary company: A$342.00 (From 1 July 2026 (up from A$329))
Fee: Director ID: A$0.00 (Free to apply)
Contact: ASIC: 1300 300 630, https://www.asic.gov.au/about-asic/contact-us
Contact: Australian Business Registry Services (director IDs): 13 62 50, https://www.abrs.gov.au/director-identification-number
Contact: business.gov.au contact centre: 13 28 46, https://business.gov.au/
Watch out: Becoming a director without a director ID is an offence (60 penalty units). Applying for more than one director ID, or misrepresenting yours, can mean up to 1 year in prison.
Watch out: From 1 July 2027 companies must give their directors' IDs to ASIC.
Watch out: Late fees apply if the annual review fee is not paid within 2 months after the review date.
Watch out: Directors have legal duties under the Corporations Act 2001; understand them before you agree to act.
Watch out: A company name does not cover other trading names. Register a business name for any other name you trade under.
Watch out: Moving from sole trader to company means a new ABN for the company and transferring any business name.

[Gathered by ApprovalReady from official websites on 2026-10-11; a summary, not the source's wording] How to get: Apply for an Australian Business Number (ABN) (Australian Business Register (ABR), administered by the Australian Taxation Office (ATO) as part of Australian Business Registry Services).
An ABN is the 11-digit number that identifies your business to government and other businesses. It is free, and you need one to invoice properly, avoid having tax withheld from payments you receive, claim GST credits and get an .au domain name. You can only get one if you are carrying on, or starting, an enterprise.
Timeframe: Usually issued immediately at the end of the online application. If you get a reference number instead, the ABR aims to review it within 20 business days.
Cost: Free. Applying for an ABN through the Australian Government costs nothing; private websites that charge a fee are not required.
Before you start: Check you pass the entitlement test: you must be carrying on or starting an enterprise in Australia (or be a Corporations Act company). Signs of a business include significant commercial activity, an intention to make a profit shown by a business plan, repeated and systematic activity run in a business-like way, and relevant skill.
Before you start: You are not entitled to an ABN for work you do as an employee (including apprentices, trade assistants and labourers, even if it is called contracting), or for a hobby. An employer should not make an ABN a condition of employment.
Before you start: If you have not started trading yet, you should already have taken some start-up steps, such as advertising, setting up a website or social media, getting licences or insurance, leasing premises or equipment, giving quotes or applying for finance.
Before you start: Choose your business structure first (sole trader, partnership, company or trust). It changes what the application asks and which other registrations you need, and changing structure later can mean a new ABN.
Before you start: Have your tax file number (TFN) ready, plus the TFNs of any associates such as partners, directors or trustees. Being identifiable from your TFN speeds the application up.
Before you start: Have ready: the date you need the ABN from (no more than six months in the future), your entity's legal name, business address, postal address, email and phone, your main business activity, the physical locations you operate from, and your ACN if you are a company.
Before you start: Email addresses must be 5 to 200 characters with no spaces and must not begin with support@, sales@ or info@.
Before you start: If you use a registered tax or BAS agent, have their agent number so they can be an authorised contact.
Step 1: Confirm you are entitled to an ABN. Read the ABR entitlement guidance and make sure your activity is an enterprise, not employment or a hobby. Keep evidence (business plan, quotes, licences, insurance, lease, adviser correspondence) because the ABR can review your entitlement at any time and ask you to prove you started, or took steps to start, your business from the date on your application. Applying without entitlement can lead to prosecution.
Step 2: Gather the information the application asks for. Collect your TFN and associates' TFNs, the ABN start date, legal name, business and postal addresses, contact details, main business activity, business locations, any previous ABN, your ACN (companies), and your tax or BAS agent number if you use one. You can save a part-finished application, but missing details will likely delay your ABN.
Step 3: Apply online through the Business Registration Service. Use the Australian Government Business Registration Service at register.business.gov.au. In the same application you can also apply for a business name, GST, an Australian company, PAYG withholding, fringe benefits tax, luxury car tax, fuel tax credits and wine equalisation tax, so you only enter your details once. (time: Most applications are finished in one sitting; cost: Free; form: Business Registration Service)
Step 4: Read the outcome at the end of the form. If approved you get your 11-digit ABN on screen straight away; save or print the confirmation. If you get a reference number, the ABR needs to check your details and aims to review within 20 business days; check ABN Lookup and expect a confirmation letter within 14 days of approval. If refused, you get a refusal number and a letter within 14 days explaining why and your review rights. (time: Immediate, or up to 20 business days if reviewed)
Step 5: Keep your ABN details up to date. Update your ABN details within 28 days of becoming aware of a change. Cancel your ABN if you close or sell the business, stop operating in Australia, or change structure (for example sole trader to company, sole trader to partnership, or partnership to company), and apply for a new one for the new structure. (time: Within 28 days of a change)
Fee: ABN application: A$0.00 (Free through the Australian Business Register / Business Registration Service)
Contact: Australian Business Register (business information enquiries): 13 92 26, https://www.abr.gov.au/contact-us/contact-abr
Contact: business.gov.au contact centre: 13 28 46, https://business.gov.au/
Contact: Translating and Interpreting Service (TIS National): 13 14 50, https://www.abr.gov.au/contact-us/contact-abr
Watch out: Applying for an ABN, registering for GST or claiming GST refunds when you are not entitled can lead to prosecution or criminal charges.
Watch out: An ABN does not replace your tax file number; you still need a TFN.
Watch out: If a business you work for insists you get an ABN but treats you like an employee, you are probably not entitled to one; check the employee or contractor rules first.
Watch out: Changing structure (for example sole trader to company) usually means cancelling the old ABN and getting a new one, and you may also need to update your business name with ASIC.
Watch out: Some private websites charge to lodge an ABN application. The government application is free.

[Gathered by ApprovalReady from official websites on 2026-10-11; a summary, not the source's wording] How to get: Register a business name with ASIC (Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC)).
If you trade under any name other than your own personal name (or your company's exact name), you must register it as a business name with ASIC. Registration is national, so one registration covers every state and territory, and you choose 1 or 3 years.
Timeframe: About 10 to 15 minutes online. Confirmation usually arrives within 2 business days if you pay by credit card, or 5 business days if you pay by BPAY, EFT or bank transfer.
Cost: A$47 for 1 year or A$108 for 3 years (fees from 1 July 2026).
Before you start: You must register a business name if you run a business in Australia and are not trading under your own name. You do not need one if you are a sole trader trading under only your first name and surname, a partnership trading under all partners' names, or a company trading under its exact company name.
Before you start: You need an ABN, or an ABN reference number if your ABN application is still being processed. You can apply for both together in the Business Registration Service.
Before you start: Check the name is free on ASIC's business names register: green means available, amber means ASIC will assess it after you apply, red means it is not available.
Before you start: Also check IP Australia's TM Checker. You cannot register a name that someone already holds as a business name or trade mark, and a registered business name does not give you exclusive rights to it.
Before you start: Have an address for service of documents (an Australian street address or PO Box) and a principal place of business (an Australian street address). Email and mobile are optional but email is where ASIC sends official notices and renewal reminders.
Before you start: For a joint venture, have each participant's ABN.
Step 1: Check name availability. Search ASIC's business names register (green, amber or red result) and IP Australia's TM Checker. If the name is close to an existing trade mark, choose another name or get advice, because the business name register does not protect you against a trade mark owner. (time: A few minutes; cost: Free)
Step 2: Get your ABN or ABN reference number. The business name must be held by an entity with an ABN. If you do not have one yet, apply for the ABN and the business name together in the Business Registration Service. (cost: Free; form: Business Registration Service)
Step 3: Apply and pay online. Apply through the Business Registration Service or ASIC's online business name registration. Choose a 1-year or 3-year period, enter your service and principal place of business addresses, and pay. Registration takes effect once the application is submitted and payment clears (up to 24 hours), and ASIC then emails your record of registration. (time: Usually within 2 business days (card) or 5 business days (BPAY, EFT, bank transfer); cost: A$47 (1 year) or A$108 (3 years); form: Business Registration Service)
Step 4: Keep your details current. Tell ASIC about changes to your registration details, usually within 28 days. If your business structure changes and you get a new ABN, the business name must be moved to the new holder. (time: Usually within 28 days of a change)
Step 5: Renew before it lapses. ASIC emails a renewal notice at least 30 days before your renewal date. Renew online through ASIC Connect or 'Pay now'. If you hold several business names or a company, you can ask ASIC to align renewal dates. If you do not renew on time, ASIC may cancel the name and someone else could register it. (time: Notice arrives at least 30 days before renewal; cost: A$47 (1 year) or A$108 (3 years))
Fee: Register or renew a business name for 1 year: A$47.00 (From 1 July 2026 (up from A$45))
Fee: Register or renew a business name for 3 years: A$108.00 (From 1 July 2026 (up from A$104))
Contact: ASIC: 1300 300 630, https://www.asic.gov.au/about-asic/contact-us
Contact: business.gov.au contact centre: 13 28 46, https://business.gov.au/
Watch out: Trading under an unregistered business name is not allowed if the name is not your own name.
Watch out: A registered business name gives you no exclusive rights. Only a registered trade mark does.
Watch out: If you miss renewal, ASIC may cancel the name and it can become available to others.
Watch out: ASIC publishes warnings about scams impersonating ASIC. Renew only through ASIC Connect or ASIC's own payment links.
Watch out: Business names are registered nationally; you do not register again with your state or territory.

Before you start: You also need GST registration if you want to claim fuel tax credits.
Before you start: The ATO says people earning through the sharing economy or digital platforms may also need to register; check the ATO's sharing economy guidance for your activity.
Before you start: GST turnover is your total business income (not profit), minus GST in your sales, certain sales to associates, input-taxed sales, sales not connected with an enterprise, and sales not connected with Australia. Before you start: If you register voluntarily, you generally must stay registered for at least 12 months.

Timeframe: No official processing times are published. Applications go through a completeness check, technical assessment, risk assessment and delegate review; incomplete applications get a request for information, which adds delay.
Cost: No permit fee is mentioned on the Defence pages read.
Before you start: Check whether your item is on the DSGL. Part 1 (Munitions List, ML1 to ML22 plus ML901 to ML910) covers items specially designed or modified for military use. Part 2 (Dual-use List, categories 0 to 9, each split into goods, test equipment, materials, software and technology) covers commercial items that could have military or WMD uses.
Before you start: Use the self-help DSGL tool in the MADE portal to check control status and get recommended forms.
Before you start: Even items not on the DSGL can be caught by 'catch-all' controls if there is a suspected military end-use or WMD link. Contact Defence for advice if in doubt.
Before you start: Intangible supply counts: Defence has separate permit guidance for supplying DSGL technology and software intangibly, supplying it to a foreign person within Australia, certain supplies from outside Australia, and providing DSGL services outside Australia.
Before you start: You need a Defence Export Controls Client Registration Number (DCRN) before you apply. Registration needs a valid ABN or an ABF Cargo Client ID (CCID), and each contact needs their own email address.
Before you start: Australian residents log in to MADE through ServiceConnect with a Digital ID such as myID; others use direct login.
Before you start: Gather end-user and consignee details, a precise technical description of the goods or technology, and shipment quantities. Vague descriptions and missing end-user details are the most common reasons for delays.
Before you start: For trade with the United States and United Kingdom, check whether you can use the AUKUS licence-free environment instead of a permit (you must be approved and lodge a notification of intent to export).
Step 1: Classify your goods, software or technology. Check the DSGL (2024 edition is current) using the MADE self-help tool. Note the control code. Proposed DSGL changes were under review in 2026.
Step 2: Register for a DCRN in the MADE portal. Log in to the My Australian Defence Exports (MADE) portal and apply for a Defence Export Controls Client Registration Number using your ABN or CCID.
Step 3: Choose the right permit type. Options include permits to export or supply military or dual-use goods or technology (including transhipment and repair or return), permits to supply to a foreign person in Australia, multi-party (project) permits, permits to match contracts, permits for items with in-principle approval, and renewals. Brokering needs broker registration and permits. Choosing the wrong application type is a common error.
Step 4: Lodge the application in MADE. All applications must be completed through MADE. Attach supporting documents (not password protected, no special characters in fields). For permits matched to a contract, give the contract name, expiry date and documentary evidence. (cost: No fee stated)

Watch out: Common reasons for delays: wrong application type, special characters in fields, password-protected attachments, vague goods descriptions, and missing consignee or end-user details.
Watch out: If you find you have breached the rules, Defence encourages voluntary disclosure.

[Gathered by ApprovalReady from official websites on 2026-10-11; a summary, not the source's wording] How to get: Lodge an export declaration and get an Export Declaration Number (EDN) (Australian Border Force (ABF), Department of Home Affairs).
Before goods leave Australia you must report them to the Australian Border Force on an export declaration if they are worth more than A$2,000, need an export permit (whatever their value), are claiming duty drawback, or are dutiable goods with duty unpaid. An accepted declaration gives you an Export Declaration Number (EDN), your authority from the ABF to deal with the goods for export.
Timeframe: You can lodge up to six months before the export date. If goods are not exported within 30 days of the intended date, withdraw the declaration within the next seven days.
Cost: The ABF pages do not list a fee for lodging an export declaration, and there are no customs duties on exports. If you use a customs broker or freight forwarder they charge their own fee (not set by government).
Before you start: Check whether you need one: goods worth more than A$2,000, goods needing an export permit (any value), goods where you claim duty drawback, and dutiable or excisable goods with duty or excise unpaid.
Before you start: Check whether an exemption applies: personal effects, pets, goods (including mail) under A$2,000, some temporary imports under section 162A of the Customs Act 1901, diplomatic bags, Australian aircraft and ship spares, Australian Government military goods for the ADF, Australian domestic cargo, and containers for international carriage.
Before you start: Check whether your goods need an export permit, for example agricultural goods (Department of Agriculture), defence and dual-use goods (Defence Export Controls), wildlife (EPBC permits), or other prohibited exports.
Before you start: Decide who will lodge. The consignor (exporter, owner of the goods, or an agent for them) lodges. The ABF recommends using a licensed customs broker or agent.
Before you start: If you lodge yourself, you need access to the Integrated Cargo System (ICS) and your ABN registered with the ABF, or you can lodge a paper form at an ABF counter with proof of identity and a client registration form if required.
Before you start: Have the details ready: consignee, final destination country, intended export date, mode of transport, port of loading, Australian Harmonized Export Commodity Classification (AHECC) code, goods description and FOB value for each line.
Before you start: Exports are generally GST-free if conditions are met; check the ATO rules.
Before you start: Keep all documents for five years after lodging.
Step 1: Confirm a declaration is required. Use the ABF 'Export requirements' page to confirm whether the value, permit, drawback or duty rules require a declaration, or whether an exemption applies.
Step 2: Get any export permit first. If your goods need an export permit, get it before you lodge, because permitted goods need an EDN whatever their value and the permit details go on the declaration.
Step 3: Lodge the export declaration. Lodge electronically through the Integrated Cargo System (ICS), usually through a customs broker. Or lodge an Export Declaration (B957) form, with the B957a supplementary page if needed, at an ABF counter in your state or territory, with original or certified evidence of identity. One declaration covers one consignment (one consignor to one consignee). (time: Up to six months before export; cost: No ABF fee listed; form: B957 Export declaration)
Step 4: Receive your EDN. The ABF outcome is an authority to deal with the goods (your EDN), an authority with conditions, or a refusal. Keep the EDN with your shipping records; you must keep documents for five years.
Step 5: Amend or withdraw if plans change. Lodge amendments as soon as possible, the same way you lodged the declaration. If goods are not exported within 30 days of the intended date, withdraw the declaration within seven days after that 30-day period (electronically or with form B611). Lodge a new declaration if you export later. (time: Withdraw within 7 days after the 30-day window)
Contact: ABF Cargo Systems Support (ICS help): https://www.abf.gov.au/help-and-support/ics/integrated-cargo-system-(ics)/using-the-ics/contact-cargo-systems-support
Contact: ABF general enquiries: https://www.abf.gov.au/importing-exporting-and-manufacturing/exporting/how-to-export/export-declaration
Watch out: Not withdrawing a declaration within the required seven days is an offence.
Watch out: Goods that need an export permit need an EDN even if they are worth less than A$2,000.
Watch out: Lodge a separate declaration for each consignment (each consignor-to-consignee shipment).
Watch out: If any details change, lodge an amendment as soon as possible, the same way you lodged the original.
Watch out: Keep commercial documents for five years after lodging; the ABF can ask for them.
Watch out: Some exporters can become 'Confirming Exporters' to declare estimates and confirm later (form B111), but only for certain goods.

The Export Market Development Grants program reimburses part of what small and medium Australian businesses spend on export marketing, as matched funding of A$20,000 up to A$80,000 a year depending on tier. Round 4 (covering 2025-26 and 2026-27) is closed, so the practical step now is to get eligible and prepare for the next round.
Timeframe: Applications are only accepted when a round is open. Round 4 opened 12 November 2024 and tiers closed when funding ran out (Tier 2 closed the same day). No date for a next round was published on the pages read.
Cost: No application fee is mentioned. You must be able to spend at least A$20,000 of your own money a year on eligible activities and match the grant amount with your own funds.
Before you start: Tier 1 (ready to export, A$20,000 up to A$30,000 a year): turnover more than A$100,000 and less than A$20 million, you have not exported before, and you have completed Austrade-recognised export training and/or the Export Readiness Test. Maximum 2 years of Tier 1.
Before you start: Tier 2 (expanding in existing markets, A$20,000 up to A$50,000 a year): turnover more than A$500,000 and less than A$20 million, with evidence of recent export sales. Maximum 4 years of Tier 2.
Before you start: Tier 3 (moving into new key markets, A$20,000 up to A$80,000 a year): turnover more than A$1 million and less than A$20 million, evidence of recent export sales, and a plan to enter one of 27 listed key economies (for example Japan, Singapore, the United States) where you do not already export. Maximum 4 years of Tier 3.
Before you start: All tiers: a valid ABN you have traded under for at least 2 years, tax compliance, products of substantially Australian origin, and capacity to spend at least A$20,000 a year of your own (non-government) money, excluding the grant.
Before you start: You can receive EMDG for up to 8 financial years in total (not necessarily consecutive). From Round 4, any year covered by a grant agreement counts, even if you report nil activity.
Before you start: Eligible activities include keeping an overseas representative, short export promotion trips, consultants for research or promotion, foreign buyer visits, free samples to potential foreign buyers, and intellectual property rights. Tier 1 can include export training.
Before you start: Get a Government Digital Identity and set up EMDG portal access early; Austrade says to give yourself plenty of time.
Step 1: Check your tier and read the guidelines. Compare your turnover and export history with the Tier 1, 2 and 3 criteria and read the EMDG grant guidelines.
Step 2: Tier 1 only: complete export training or the Export Readiness Test. Before applying for Tier 1 you must complete Austrade-recognised export training and/or the Export Readiness Test and keep the evidence. (time: Before applying)
Step 3: Prepare your plan to market and evidence. Download the sample application form and write a plan to market using the mandatory template; it must be specific to your business. Gather your ABN and proof of 2 years trading, ANZSIC code, proof of tax compliance (such as a business activity statement), evidence of Australian origin, and evidence of turnover and capacity to spend and match funds. (time: Before the round opens)
Step 4: Apply in the EMDG online portal when a round opens. Log in with your Digital Identity and lodge. Applications are assessed in the order received and tiers close when funding is fully allocated, so be ready on opening day. Not all applicants are funded. (time: When the next round opens)
Step 5: If funded: submit milestone reports. Your grant agreement sets milestone report due dates and payment schedules. For Round 4, the portal opened on 3 August 2026 for milestone reports covering 2026-27 spending. Required evidence is in Section E of your grant agreement. (time: As set in your grant agreement)
Contact: Austrade EMDG: 13 28 78, emdg.help@austrade.gov.au, https://www.austrade.gov.au/en/how-we-can-help-you/grants/export-market-development-grants

Watch out: Your plan to market must be specific to your business; copied or generic plans are not accepted.
Watch out: Years under a grant agreement count towards your 8-year lifetime limit even if you claim nothing.
Watch out: Tier 3 markets must be new to you; markets where you already have sales do not count.
Watch out: Not all eligible applicants receive funding; applications are assessed in the order received until each tier's funding runs out.
